1033.d:
Overlapping rings of lines spin to create mesmerizing, meditative moiré patterns. The longer you watch, the more the colors mix to create wild blends and waves of iridescence before meeting back up where it started in a perfect loop. If you look long enough, you may even see impossible colors. 

The colors follow a color scheme (split complementary, analogous, square, triad, or monochromatic) to ensure the colors blend well together. 

About 1% of the pieces will be ghosted, meaning the color is almost entirely drained out, creating an eery, ethereal look. These are the rarest ones.  

The gradient mode dictates how the colors in-between the scheme are generated. "Direct Path" is a simple gradient between the colors, while "Color wheel walk" means the hue "walked" the color wheel to get to its next color likely picking up other colors along the way. 

Other traits are the skew angle of the lines, the speed of the rotation, and the size of the ring.

These look even better full screen.

1051.d:
This generative braid artwork is built in plain JavaScript, and is based on code I wrote several years ago, here updated with new aesthetics and features. This work is motivated by a beautiful mathematical structure called a braid group.

Each unique mint of the token chooses randomized parameters with varying probability weights for the number of strings, their spacing, coloring schemes and resulting color palettes, and crossing sizes, angles and frequency.

Colors are randomly generated from an algorithm, including the background color. Most of the pieces (70% probability) will feature colors from two separate hue intervals; a smaller number (20%) use only one color interval, and even more rare are the Black-White-Color palettes (6%), and the Black-and-White palette (4%).

Most of them scroll up, but approximately 7% of them scroll down.

The braid will endlessly scroll without any repetition in its pattern.

Dan Gries
Twitter: @rectangleworld

Pattern: The walk style, with "Static" being the rarest.

Shape: The drawing element, either ellipse or, someone less likely, rectangle.

1095.d:
This is a journey through architecture that never existed.

Inspired by the grammatical rules behind French sacral architecture of the Middle Ages, this generative tool is meant for creating a collection of 256 plans of fictional buildings. Each plan is a unique variation on semantic relations between architectural elements: from a regular composition resembling existing churches to a dynamic aggregation of vaults, columns and chevets. But always following the same set of rules extracted from multiple examples of gothic cathedrals.

Every church has its place and time in which it could have been built in an alternative series of historical events.

This artistic tribute to the research of Stiny and Mitchell about Palladian architecture or Duarte's work about Siza takes the topic of formalizing architectural language onto a lighthearted level by moving it to a slightly imaginary world.

To zoom, press a mouse button when over the image or touch the screen. To pan, keep the mouse pressed and move it around.

1109.d:
The drawing of leaves is a little special. It uses fractal. The method is to start with an equilateral triangle, divide each edge into three equal parts, and then take the middle length of each edge as the bottom edge. Make regular triangles outward respectively, and then erase the "bottom" line segment, so as to get a hexagon with 12 sides. Then divide each side into three equal parts, take the length of each middle part as the bottom edge, make an equilateral triangle outward, and erase the bottom line segment. Repeat this process, you will get a picture of "leaves".
Recursive algorithm is used in the code.

1184.d:
A fun piece, a little different from my usual output. What could be more unique than your own hash, duplicated and mapped onto a sphere? A true one-of-a-kind generative piece of art.

The hash is taken, split in half, duplicated, recombined and mapped onto a sphere, lit from three directions by appropriate lighting using the magic of Processing.

Colours are selected randomly, with a small chance for greyscale included, and there's also the rare possibility of a tiny orbiting moon that actually is a moon, not a miniature Deathstar.
